title: An always-on personal ops agent
intent: I want Hermes running 24/7, handling my inbox, calendar and daily errands without me prompting it

stack.why: Headless systemd deployment, which is what an agent that has to survive reboots and run overnight crons actually needs.
An official Hermes memory provider — the difference between an agent that re-learns your preferences daily and one that remembers them.
Gives the agent WebDAV/CalDAV hands on real calendar, task and contact data instead of a chat-only surface.
A 24/7 agent is only useful if you can check on it from your phone, and this is a web UI built for exactly that rather than a desktop app you have to be at.
Attributes usage and estimated cost per scheduled run, so a silently looping cron shows up as a line item instead of a surprise bill.

rationale: This is the single most common thing people actually do with Hermes, and it is not one tool — it is a host that never sleeps, a memory that outlives the session, at least one real-world integration to act on, and a way to look in from your phone. Start with the host and memory; those two decide whether the rest is worth wiring. Add the calendar/task integration once the agent is stable, because that is the first place a hallucinated action has real consequences. Cron analytics comes last but comes early enough to catch the runaway schedule before the invoice does.
caveats: Scheduled runs are where cost quietly compounds — instrument before you scale up the cron count, not after.
Giving an agent write access to a live calendar or task list is the first genuinely destructive capability in this stack. Run it read-only for a week first.

title: Hermes in your pocket
intent: I want to talk to my Hermes agent from my phone — mobile app, web UI, or a messaging bridge

stack.why: The default answer for phone access — a browser UI with terminal parity, no app-store round trip.
Native SwiftUI app that pairs with a self-hosted hermes-webui, if a web view on iOS isn't good enough for you.
Chat, terminal and device control over WSS, for the Android side of the same problem.
A mobile-first Telegram Mini App dashboard — Telegram is by far the most common messaging bridge in the story corpus.
One-command installer if you'd rather run the agent on the phone than reach a server from it.

rationale: There are two genuinely different answers here and people conflate them. Either the agent runs on a server and your phone is a client, or the agent runs on the phone. The server-plus-client path is what almost everyone ends up on, so start with hermes-webui and only reach for a native client if the web view specifically annoys you. Pick the messaging bridge based on where you already live — Telegram dominates the corpus, but the same shape works elsewhere. The on-device install is a real option, not a toy, but it is a different set of tradeoffs around battery, background execution and model cost.
caveats: Exposing a self-hosted agent to the internet for phone access is the most common way people accidentally publish a shell. Tunnel it (Tailscale or equivalent) rather than opening a port.
Native mobile clients pair with a specific backend — check the pairing requirement before assuming any client works with your setup.

title: A coding agent that actually knows your codebase
intent: I want Hermes to understand my repo deeply instead of re-reading files and burning tokens every session

stack.why: A local pre-indexed knowledge graph built specifically to cut the token usage and tool-call churn of agents groping through a repo.
Long-term, cross-project memory for coding agents, so what the agent learned in one repo isn't lost when you switch.
Tree-sitter, ast-grep and LSP bridge tools — structural code operations instead of regex-and-hope.
The most-adopted agentic skills framework in the catalog; it supplies the how-to-work-on-code layer above raw retrieval.
A local trace viewer for the agent's API traffic — the fastest way to see why a session went sideways.

rationale: The complaint behind this use case is almost never "the model is dumb" — it is "the agent keeps rediscovering my repo from scratch." So the stack is ordered by how much of that waste each layer removes. Indexing the code once (codegraph) removes the most. Persisting what was learned across sessions and projects (agentcairn) removes the next chunk. AST-aware tools cut the remaining flailing on structural edits. The skills framework changes how the agent approaches the work rather than what it can see, and the trace viewer is how you find out which of the above isn't earning its keep.
caveats: Indexing and memory layers both add a staleness problem: an index that lags your working tree produces confidently wrong answers. Check the reindex trigger before trusting it on a fast-moving branch.
These layers overlap. Adding all five at once makes it very hard to tell which one helped — introduce them one at a time.

title: Cut your token bill
intent: I want to know where my spend is going and run Hermes for a fraction of what it costs me now

stack.why: CLI token-usage tracking across Hermes and the other agent CLIs — you cannot cut what you haven't measured.
Real-time token, cost and rate-limit readout that reads Hermes state directly, for the during-the-session view.
Reduces tool-schema overhead via keyword selection — this targets the per-call fixed cost that people are consistently shocked by.
Budget enforcement, not just observability — it stops runaway costs rather than reporting them afterwards.
Running the agent on an Android handset via Termux is a genuinely used answer to "I don't want to pay for a server."

rationale: Every cost story in the corpus follows the same arc: someone measures, discovers the bill is mostly fixed overhead rather than useful work, and then attacks that. So measure before you optimize — tokscale for the ledger, token-monitor for the live view. The single biggest lever people report is trimming what gets sent every call (tool schemas, context), which is what the slimmer targets. Add hard budget enforcement before you add more automation, because scheduled work is where spend compounds while you aren't looking. Cheaper hosting is real savings but it is the smallest term; do it last.
caveats: Trimming tool schemas trades capability for cost — the agent can only use tools it can still see. Verify your critical workflows after slimming.
Enforcement plugins that hard-stop on budget will interrupt long-running jobs mid-flight. Decide whether you want a ceiling or an alarm.

title: A multi-agent build pipeline
intent: I want several agents planning, coding, reviewing and shipping in parallel instead of one agent doing everything serially

stack.why: Self-hosted orchestration that dispatches tasks, runs multi-agent workflows and monitors spend in one place.
Create, supervise and review autonomous Hermes work from one screen — the review half is what keeps a fleet from shipping garbage.
Aggregates sessions across Hermes, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, for when the fleet isn't all one agent.
Multi-step execution with checkpoints and recovery — the difference between a failed run you can resume and one you restart.
Review gates, parallel groups and auto-verify, so agents follow the plan rather than improvising past it.

rationale: Fleets fail on coordination, not capability. The stories that work all have the same two things: a single screen where you can see what every agent is doing, and a gate the work has to pass before it lands. So the orchestrator and the review surface come first, together — an orchestrator without review just produces bad work faster. Checkpointing matters more than it sounds like it should, because long parallel runs fail partway and restarting from zero is what kills the economics. Plan enforcement is the last piece and the one people add after their first agent confidently does the wrong task well.
caveats: Parallel agents multiply spend linearly and mistakes faster than that. Pair this stack with the cost-visibility one before scaling past a handful of lanes.
Several of these tools assume they own the session lifecycle. Running two orchestrators at once is a common and confusing failure.

title: A fully self-hosted, private stack
intent: I want Hermes running entirely on my own hardware with local models and no data leaving my network

stack.why: A simple Docker sandbox image — the least-effort way to stop an autonomous agent from having your whole machine.
A fully-local multi-model framework running on consumer GPUs with Ollama, so inference stays on your hardware too.
On-device memory and context with no cloud dependency — memory is the layer that sees everything, so a cloud-backed provider here would quietly undo the rest of the stack.
A security harness for PII and credentials, which matters more, not less, once everything is inside your own perimeter.
A self-hosted web interface so the private stack is still pleasant to use without reaching for a hosted dashboard.

rationale: "Self-hosted" quietly breaks at whichever layer you forget. People containerize the agent, run a local model, and then wire in a cloud memory provider — and the private stack has a cloud dependency in the one place that sees everything. So this bundle is deliberately ordered by where the leaks actually happen: runtime, then inference, then memory. The safety layer is not optional just because the network is yours; the credential and PII exposure is from the agent to itself. Everything here has a heavier local-hardware cost than the cloud equivalent, and that tradeoff is the whole point.
caveats: Local models are meaningfully weaker at long tool-use chains. Expect to simplify workflows that worked on a frontier model.
Sandboxing and remote access pull in opposite directions — decide your access story (tunnel, not open port) before you harden the runtime.
gaps: The catalog has no strong self-hosted, local-first web-search option yet — community stories reach for a self-run SearXNG container, which isn't in Atlas as a Hermes-specific project.

title: Your notes as the agent's second brain
intent: I want Hermes to read and write my Obsidian vault as its long-term memory, not a black-box database

stack.why: Explicitly built around using your own Obsidian vault as the memory substrate rather than an opaque vector store.
A DAG-based context engine that never drops a message — the failure people hit when compaction silently eats their constraints.
Re-asserts standing instructions after context compaction, detecting drift and rehydrating before the model answers.
A native workspace with an actual memory browser, so 'what does it think it knows' is a question you can answer.

rationale: The recurring complaint in these stories is not that the agent forgets — it is that you cannot see or edit what it remembers. Plain-markdown memory fixes that at the root: the vault is human-readable, diffable and yours. But file-backed memory alone doesn't survive long sessions, which is why the context engine and the compaction guard are in the bundle rather than optional extras; losing standing instructions mid-session is the specific failure people describe. The memory browser closes the loop by making the agent's state inspectable instead of inferred from its behavior.
caveats: Markdown memory scales worse than a vector store on retrieval quality once the vault gets large. This is a legibility-over-recall trade, made deliberately.
Giving an agent write access to a vault you care about warrants a git-backed vault and a review habit.

title: A content engine that writes in your voice
intent: I want Hermes researching, drafting and posting content that actually sounds like me

stack.why: An official memory provider — your past writing is the training data for your voice, and it has to persist across sessions.
Transcript, search, channel and playlist skills — the most common research input in the content stories.
A content production plugin with explicit quality gates and AI-pattern humanization, rather than a single drafting prompt.
Audits and rewrites to strip detectable AI writing patterns — the step that decides whether the output is publishable.
Native X automation, for the last mile that otherwise stays manual.

rationale: The stories that produce content people actually ship all separate three things that beginners collapse into one prompt: what to write about, how you sound, and whether it reads as machine-written. Memory carries your voice, because voice is a corpus problem and not a prompt problem. The research skills feed the topic pipeline. The production plugin and the de-slop pass are the quality gate, and they are the reason the output is publishable rather than merely generated. Automated publishing goes last, deliberately — it is the step you should trust least early on.
caveats: Automated posting is publishing. Keep a human approval step until the voice is genuinely right; a bad post is not retractable.
Platform automation depends on third-party API access that changes without warning — expect maintenance on the publishing layer specifically.

title: A generative media studio
intent: I want Hermes generating images, video, music and visuals, not just text

stack.why: Fronts GPT Image 2, Nanobanana and ComfyUI behind one plugin, with a large prompt library — one integration instead of three.
Official FLUX skills carrying prompting guidelines and API integration, so image quality comes from documented technique rather than trial and error.
A portable Windows desktop bundling local models, TTS, music and ComfyUI — the practical answer when generation volume makes per-call API pricing painful.
A TTS provider with native voice-message delivery, for the speech half of creative work rather than the visual half.
A local-first design and prototyping system with coding-agent CLI support, for turning generated assets into an actual layout.

rationale: Creative work is where the community is most inventive and least served by any single tool, so this bundle is deliberately a toolbox rather than a pipeline. Start with the image hub, because one plugin fronting several backends beats wiring each generator separately, and pair it with real prompting technique — the gap between a mediocre generation and a good one is almost always the prompt, not the model. Local generation matters more here than anywhere else in the catalog: creative work is iterative by nature, and per-call pricing punishes iteration hardest. Voice and design sit alongside rather than after, depending on whether you are making something to hear or something to look at.
caveats: Generation volume is where creative projects get expensive. Decide local-versus-API before you build the loop, not after the first bill.
Model and API surfaces in this space change faster than anywhere else in the catalog — expect the generation layer to need maintenance.
gaps: The community stories lean heavily on TouchDesigner, ComfyUI workflows and RenPy, but those live as personal skills rather than catalog projects — Atlas has no dedicated video-generation or generative-visuals entry yet.

title: A daily research briefing
intent: I want Hermes to scan sources overnight and hand me a filtered briefing every morning

stack.why: Auto-routes across Serper, Tavily, Exa, Querit and Perplexity, so one provider being down or rate-limited doesn't kill the run.
A second search-and-retrieval path over MCP — briefings that run unattended need redundancy more than they need peak quality.
Transcripts and channel search pull in a source class that pure web search misses entirely.

stack.role: Remember what it already told you
stack.why: Retain/recall/reflect workflows so day 30's briefing doesn't repeat day 1's findings.
Cron-based research ingestion with cost forecasting on a headless systemd host — the unattended-execution half of the problem.

rationale: A briefing agent is a reliability problem dressed as a research problem. It runs while you sleep, so anything that can fail silently will, and you find out by receiving nothing. That is why there are two search paths here rather than the single best one, and why scheduled ingestion is treated as its own component instead of a cron line. Memory is what separates a briefing from an RSS reader: without it the agent has no notion of what it already told you, and the signal-to-noise collapses in the second week.
caveats: Search-provider APIs are the usual failure point and most are paid. Check quota behavior before pointing a daily cron at them.
Deduplicating against prior briefings is the hard part and no tool here does it for free — expect to tune it.

title: An agent that can actually browse the web
intent: I want Hermes to search, scrape and drive a real browser instead of answering from training data

stack.why: Cloudflare Browser Rendering for crawling, scraping and extracting page content — the cheap path that covers most of what people actually mean by “read the web”.
Multi-provider search with auto-routing, because scraping only helps once the agent knows which URL to open.
A browser built for autonomous agent control over MCP rather than for a human operator — it was born at the Nous hackathon for exactly this problem.
An MCP service that operates a real Chrome instance with page scanning, CDP, screenshots and synthetic input, for sites a scraper cannot satisfy.
A Chromium side-panel extension that hands your active browser context to a local or remote Hermes runtime, when the page needs a session you are already logged into.
Bundles web search, social and on-chain data behind a single plugin — the answer to accumulating a separate API key per source.

rationale: People say “browse the web” to mean three different capabilities, and picking the wrong one wastes the most time here. Fetching and extracting a known page is the cheapest and covers the majority of real tasks, so start there. Search is what makes fetching useful, because an agent that cannot find the URL cannot read it. Only when a site genuinely resists extraction — heavy JavaScript, real interaction, a login — do you need a browser under agent control, and that is a large step up in both cost and fragility. The extension is the honest answer to authenticated pages: rather than teaching an agent your credentials, lend it a session you already have.
caveats: Driving a real browser is far more fragile and expensive than fetching a page. Reach for it when extraction has actually failed, not by default.
Handing an agent your logged-in browser session is the most consequential permission in this stack — it inherits everything you are authenticated to.
Scraping at volume runs into bot detection and terms of service well before it runs into technical limits.
gaps: Atlas has no dedicated credential or session manager for agent browsing yet — today that risk is managed by choosing which browser context you lend, not by a tool.

title: Run Hermes for a team or clients
intent: I want to operate Hermes for a team or for paying clients, with isolation, oversight and cost attribution

stack.why: A template for going from one VPS agent to specialist teams and orchestrated workflows — the shape this use case converges on.
A community Helm chart with state-safety guardrails, for when 'one VPS' stops being the answer.
A self-hostable mission-control dashboard backed by your own Postgres, so client work is reviewable rather than trusted.
A shared memory layer with an open format, so a team of agents has common ground instead of N private silos.
Budget enforcement and observability — necessary the moment spend has to be attributed to a client rather than to you.

rationale: The business-ops stories converge on one pattern: isolate per client, watch everything, and be able to say what each engagement cost. Isolation comes first because it is the thing you cannot retrofit — the people running this successfully describe one profile or one instance per client from day one. Orchestration and a real dashboard follow, because selling agent work means being able to show the work. Shared memory is the subtle one: it is what lets a team of agents behave like a team, and it is also the boundary you must not accidentally cross between clients.
caveats: Client isolation is a hard boundary. Shared memory across agents is valuable within one engagement and a serious problem across two — scope it explicitly.
Running someone else's business on an autonomous agent changes the risk profile entirely. Pair this with the guardrails bundle before it touches anything billable.
gaps: Atlas has no dedicated multi-tenant billing or per-client cost-attribution project yet — today this is assembled from general telemetry plus per-client isolation.

title: Guardrails before it touches anything real
intent: I want approval gates and sandboxing so my agent can't do something destructive on its own

stack.why: Sandboxing with hardware-level enforcement — the outermost boundary, and the one that holds when the others are misconfigured.
A runtime security layer for sensitive credentials and PII, catching the exfiltration class rather than the destruction class.
A fork with integrated CaMeL trust boundaries for safer autonomous execution, if you want this at the agent level rather than bolted on.
Guard policies and risk assessment — the layer that decides which actions need a human before they run.
Parallel subagents attacking the change from different angles before it lands, for the code path specifically.

rationale: Almost every guardrail story starts the same way — the agent did something confidently wrong, fast, and the person went looking for a brake. Layer these from outside in: a sandbox that limits the blast radius regardless of what the agent believes, a runtime harness for the credentials it can see, then policy that decides which actions require a human. The trust-boundary fork is the alternative to bolting the middle layers on, and it is a real fork, so treat it as an either/or rather than an addition. Adversarial review is narrower — it protects the code you ship, not the system the agent runs on.
caveats: A fork with built-in trust boundaries and a bolted-on harness solve overlapping problems. Pick one architecture rather than stacking both.
Guardrails only bind the paths they know about. An agent with shell access routes around policy that lives above the shell.

title: See what your agent is actually doing
intent: I want visibility into every tool call, session and decision instead of guessing from the output

stack.why: A local viewer for the agent's actual API traffic — ground truth when the output and your mental model disagree.
Read-only observability with journeys and reports, so instrumenting the agent can't itself change its behavior.
OpenTelemetry export, so agent traces land in whatever you already use rather than a bespoke dashboard.
A native session browser and analytics view — the after-the-fact question of what happened last Tuesday.
Discovery, monitoring and auto-recovery for multi-agent systems, for setups where noticing late is itself the failure.

rationale: There are three distinct questions here and picking the wrong tool for yours wastes a weekend: what is it doing right now, what did it do last week, and why did this specific call go wrong. The trace viewer answers the third and is the one people reach for during an incident. Read-only journeys and session history answer the first two, and the read-only property matters more than it sounds — observability that mutates the agent's context is a debugging trap. OTel export is the escape hatch if you already have infrastructure; auto-recovery is only worth it once you have enough agents that watching them manually stopped working.
caveats: Full tool-call logging captures whatever the agent saw, secrets included. Treat the trace store as sensitive.
Several of these overlap heavily. Start with the one matching your actual question rather than installing the set.
